status: IDENTIFIED VIA PORTFOLIO GAP ANALYSIS (Jul. 30, 2026) — NOT YET FILED. Third First Advantage furnishing now documented: Order WPS-361214148 consumer disclosure (Sep. 15, 2026) to TASKUS HOLDINGS INC USA with SOURCE OF RECORD: CALIFORNIA SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY (Matter 40). Additive to the FedEx (25) and UPS (26) registry-flagged reports. No demand letter yet.
key_facts: First Advantage (fadv.com) is the background-screening vendor that ran the pre-employment background check underlying both Matter 25 (Newanforbi v. Federal Express Corporation) and Matter 26 (Newanforbi v. United Parcel Service, Inc.), and it is First Advantage — not the employer — that generated and transmitted every notice in both adverse-action sequences under its own letterhead (DoNotReply@fadv.com). A third First Advantage employment screen for TaskUs (Matter 40) produced Order WPS-361214148: consumer disclosure letter dated Sep. 15, 2026 to TASKUS HOLDINGS INC USA encloses an NSOR hit stating SOURCE OF RECORD: CALIFORNIA SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY; SENTENCE: REGISTERED SEX OFFENDER — the same source architecture as the FedEx and UPS reports. Cover letter says the results are not acceptance or rejection; no TaskUs adverse-action letter is in the portfolio yet. For UPS: Pre Adverse Action Notification, July 22, 2024, 9:57 AM, followed by reminder notices July 23 and July 27, 2024, and a Final Adverse Action Notification July 31, 2024, 9:57 AM. For FedEx: Pre-Adverse Employment Action Notice, March 10, 2025, 1:44 PM, a duplicate notice March 11, 2025 to a second email address, five further reminder notices between March 11 and March 16, 2025, and a final Adverse Employment Action Notice March 19, 2025, 1:47 PM. Both sequences follow an identical template and cadence roughly eight months apart, and both are alleged (on information and belief, per Matters 25/26) to have disclosed Plaintiff's Megan's Law registry status — information Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E) categorically bars from employment use — to the requesting employer. Unlike Matter 29 (Amazon/Accurate Background) and the abandoned Matter 23 (Macy's/HireRight), where the vendor was named alongside the employer in a single action, First Advantage was never joined as a defendant in either Matter 25 or Matter 26, despite generating the registry-flagged report in both.
procedural_status: Not yet filed; this entry documents a gap-analysis finding, not an active case. No pre-filing demand letter has been sent to First Advantage and no complaint has been drafted. As with Matters 25/26, Plaintiff does not currently possess the underlying First Advantage background-check report from either instance — the secure portal links expired before he could preserve them — so any complaint would rely on the same documentary trail already pled on information-and-belief in Matters 25/26 (application confirmations, pre-adverse/adverse notices, reminder cadence), supplemented by discovery directed at First Advantage itself (a subpoena for the underlying reports would resolve the information-and-belief gap for all three matters at once). FCRA's limitations period (15 U.S.C. § 1681p) is the later of two years after discovery of the violation or five years after the violation itself — the earlier, UPS-related notice (July 22, 2024) sets the operative outer boundary and should be diaried independently of Matters 25/26's own deadlines. ICRAA's limitations period and proper venue/service address for First Advantage (a national CRA) should be confirmed before any filing; San Joaquin Superior Court is the natural venue given the overlapping facts and its use in Matters 25/26, but is not yet confirmed as proper for a CRA headquartered elsewhere.
damages: Not yet demanded or pled. CONSERVATIVE: ~$30,000. MODERATE: ~$89,000. AGGRESSIVE: ~$205,000. Deliberately excludes any Emotional Distress / Lost Opportunity component — that harm is already claimed against the employers in Matters 25 and 26 for these same two denials, and duplicating it here would double-count a shared injury across three dockets (the same convention the portfolio applies to the Matter 1/2/7/20 CDL wage-loss overlap). This matter's own theory is vendor-specific: ICRAA and FCRA statutory penalties for First Advantage's own furnishing conduct, not the employers' use of the reports.
risk: Favorable on the documentary pattern — the same vendor generated two registry-flagged reports for two different employers eight months apart, which supports willfulness for a CRA in a way a single instance would not. Untested in this portfolio, however: PC § 290.46(j)(4)(A)'s statutory penalty is written to reach 'any person' who uses registry information for employment purposes, and it is not yet established (here or elsewhere in the portfolio) that a CRA merely compiling and furnishing the report — rather than the employer that decided not to hire — is a 'user' within that provision; this matter is pled instead through FCRA/ICRAA vendor-liability theories to avoid that open question. Carries the same evidentiary limitation as Matters 25/26: Plaintiff does not hold the underlying report from either instance, so First Advantage's actual disclosure of registry information is currently an information-and-belief allegation pending discovery.
